newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine growers preparing gene-modified soybeans.
newsitem.headline: Argentine growers preparing gene-modified soybeans.

text.p: Argentina could start making big exports by 1998 of the genetically-modified soybeans which have sparked a European food scare and local merchants are now building up seed stocks, a top supplier said.

Argentina will probably be the second major soybean producer to follow the United States into genetically-modified soy, a product which has fueled protests by European environmental and consumer groups.
Grain merchants Nidera S.A. began developing genetically-modified soy seed in 1990 in Argentina and is now making its first sales to farmers in small quantities.
But it hopes its seed stocks will be enough to feed a large part of Argentine farmers' soy demand next season.
"I'd say the modified bean seed will surely make up a third of sales next year at least," Enrique Firpo, general manager of Nidera's seed division, told Reuters.

Argentina is one of the world's largest soybean exporters, and makes a large part of its sales to northern Europe, precisely where fears over the gene-modified soy are most acute. Soybeans find their way into a large variety of everyday foods such as mayonnaise, margarine and chocolate.

Greenpeace activists were holding up a shipment of U.S. soybeans in the port of Antwerp on Friday. Some leading European firms, including the German unit of Anglo-Dutch giant Unilever, have decided not to risk consumer wrath by using the new beans, even though they consider them safe.

Firpo said that Argentine farmers were showing great interest in the new beans, which would cut their spending on herbicide. The beans are resistant to one type of herbicide which kills all the weeds that normally plague the crop, which farmers can then use to replace a cocktail of three or four weed killers with which the fields are usually treated.
But Nidera, Argentina's biggest supplier of soybean seed, said its sales for the 1996/97 spring sowing, which is now about to start, will be "less than irrelevent".

Nidera is the only supplier of modified soybean seed in Argentina this season. It imported gene plasm from the United States and has blended the material with local soybean varieties to produce a new plant both resistant to herbicide and well adapted to Argentine conditions.
"Sales will be significant in 1997/98, and there'll be other seed merchants selling genetically-modified beans next year," Firpo said.
Argentine agricultural authorities followed the lead of U.S. agencies by approving the beans for human consumption.
